summary: Perimeter is the total distance once around the boundary of a 2-D shape — found by measuring every side and adding the lengths, or for a regular shape multiplying one side by the number of sides. The core idea to secure is that perimeter is a length (the once-around distance) and is distinct from area (the surface covered inside). Target age 7–8.
misconceptions: Adds only the two given sides of a rectangle, forgetting the opposite two.
Confuses perimeter with area — counts the squares inside instead of the distance around.
For a regular shape, measures one side but doesn't account for all the equal sides.
Gives the perimeter as a bare number without a length unit.

activities.title: Walk the boundary and build the total
steps: Trace a finger or marker all the way around the edge of a shape, starting and finishing at the same corner, so 'perimeter' is felt as walking once around and back to the start.
On a rectangle that shows only two adjacent side lengths, work out the two hidden opposite sides (opposite sides are equal), label them, then add all four sides.
Keep a running total as you cover each side, and only count the perimeter as complete when the whole boundary has been traced back to the start.
On a regular pentagon with one side labelled, find the perimeter as side length × 5 (or by adding five equal sides) and explain why the shortcut works.
Measure every side of a small irregular shape with a ruler and add the lengths.
Write each answer with its length unit (cm or m).
activities.insight: Perimeter is the complete once-around distance: you must account for every side (including hidden equal ones), it is a length with a unit, and for a regular shape equal sides let you multiply instead of adding one by one.

activities.title: Perimeter is not area
steps: On one straight-sided shape drawn along the lines of a square grid, first trace the boundary and add the side lengths to find the perimeter, then shade the interior and count the unit squares to find the area (in square units).
State in your own words which measure is a distance around the edge and which is the surface covered inside.
Given a question, decide whether it is asking for perimeter or area before you start, and say how you know.
activities.insight: Perimeter (distance around the edge, a length) and area (surface covered inside) are different measures on the very same shape and must not be swapped.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and mixed practice
steps: Solve fill-the-blank items: a rectangle with only two adjacent sides given (supply the opposite two, then total), and a regular polygon with one side labelled (use side × number of sides).
Judge a worked example where another child added only the two given rectangle sides — say what went wrong and give the correct perimeter.
Answer a mixed item where one option is the area of the shape, choosing and justifying the correct perimeter.
Check every answer carries its length unit.
activities.insight: Applying perimeter across rectangle (hidden sides), regular-polygon (side×n), and perimeter-vs-area cases, and critiquing a wrong method, consolidates accurate, unit-bearing reasoning.

checkQuestion: Give a rectangle (with only two adjacent sides labelled), a regular pentagon (one side labelled), and a small irregular shape, with a ruler. Say: 'Find the perimeter of each.' Watch whether they measure/account for every side, whether they add all sides (not just the two given), whether they confuse it with the area, and whether they keep the unit.
checkAnswer: The child finds the total distance around each shape: for the rectangle, uses all four sides (supplying the two unlabelled opposite sides); for the regular pentagon, multiplies the side by 5 (or adds five equal sides); measures every side of the irregular shape and sums them; and states each perimeter with a length unit.
